rationale: Evidence: iteration 8 (sensors at y = 0.08 m, the geometry maximum) is the best design so far at 666.2. The oval finishes 20 of 20 at 1.95 s. The s-bend finishes 19 of 20 (mean 905). The slalom still fails in all 20 trials by going off track, with progress 0.36 and about 1.05 line-loss events per run. Moving the sensors from y = 0.06 to 0.08 added only about 12 points, and the slalom progress barely moved (0.35 to 0.36), so the forward-position lever is near its limit. Earlier single-lever tests on speed, sensor spacing, sensor size and kp/kd at 3.5/1.0 did not help. The one controller change that clearly helped was adding integral action: ki 0 to 0.5 raised the oval from 808 to 927 at y = 0.03. The contract says the motors have a fixed left/right mismatch, so a residual lateral bias on the straight sections and gentle bends is plausible, and the slalom and s-bend are where bias pushes the robot to the 0.06 m limit. Change (one variable): ki 0.5 to 1.0. The integral is still capped at plus or minus 2 by the contract, so windup is bounded. Geometry, base_speed, kp, kd, weights and line_loss stay as in iteration 8. Expected result: lower lateral bias, so s-bend and slalom progress rise and s-bend completions hold or improve, with the oval still finishing near 2 s. Risk: a larger integral can cause overshoot on the s-bend sign changes, which would show as steering_oscillation above about 0.45 and a fall in s-bend completions. If that happens, the next step is ki about 0.7. Hypotheses to check: (a) a constant bias is the cause of the slalom line losses, so progress rises with ki; (b) if slalom progress does not move, the limit is the steering response (kp/kd, wheel_track or mass), not bias; (c) if the oval gets faster but the s-bend overshoots, ki is past its useful range. Next measurements: progress, line_loss_events, max_error and steering_oscillation per track, plus completion_time on the oval and s-bend.
